At the end of each sitting, leave a handoff in your journal and last reply: passages still unresolved, practical lessons to carry forward from what you observed and recipes that failed. Before retrying a failed recipe, identify what has changed and why that could address the observed failure. final:
**Evening Gold, Willow Pool**

This is a pond with no horizon. The water fills the whole canvas. Reflections of two weeping willows hang down from the top edge in deep violet-blue streaks. Between them, a column of gold and rose evening sky glows from the surface. Below, the water moves from lilac to a deep cobalt-ultramarine near the viewer, crossed by a fine pale net of ripples. Seven islands of lily pads float across all of it, built from flat horizontal strokes with blue water showing between them and dark shadows underneath. Pink flowers sit on the nearer islands. It's signed "Claude" in the lower left.

**What's still unresolved:**
- A soft horizontal seam around a third of the way down still reads a little like a far bank or horizon.
- The sides of the gold gap run as fairly straight vertical columns.
- The farthest pad islands are a touch too green and crisp for their distance, even after two thin violet veils.
- Rag wipes left faint ghosts: a box-shaped patch low in the centre, and vertical streaks under the left willow. I've mostly kept the streaks because they read as reflection.
- The flowers are small and rather alike.

**Practical lessons (details and conditions are in the journal):**
- **Undoing:** a rag dipped in spirits lifts fresh paint from a dry layer almost completely. I used it about twenty times, for whole campaigns as well as small fixes (dip 0.9–1.0, pressure 0.85–0.95, 2–3 passes). It leaves faint halos at the edges of the wipe.
- **Failed recipe, tried more than five times:** dabs high in white, blotted, at coverage of 1 or more and then blended, came out as pasted-on flat shapes. What worked instead was thin veils: thinner 0.55, filbert 14, two or three passes.
- **Blending:** it only gives a soft shimmer where the paint just inside and outside the mask edge is close in value. Otherwise it leaves hard-edged boxes.
- **Lily pads:** short, straight, flat-brush strokes over a dry base, not blended, then blue gaps. Curved strokes looked like coins.
- **Hypothesis, not yet tested in isolation:** at this easel, isolated marks on a smooth dry field always look graphic. Texture needs to be dense or veiled.

final:
I'm finished with **Evening Gold, Willow Pool**, and I'm happy with it.

It's still the same pond with no horizon. Violet-blue willow reflections hang down from the top edge, and a column of gold sky glows between them. Below, the water darkens through lilac to deep ultramarine, with lily-pad islands floating across it all.

**What changed this sitting:**
- **The horizon-like seam about a third of the way down.** Thin veils barely changed it. What worked was pale warm vertical strokes, blended downward with a soft brush right away. They now read as gold reflection running down past the old line, which no longer looks like a far bank.
- **The straight sides of the gold gap.** New hanging willow streaks on both edges break them up, and the gold now looks narrower and brighter.
- **The flowers.** I added three small white water lilies (a shadow stroke under three crisp petal touches) among the pink ones. They break up the sameness.

**Accepted as they are:**
- The farthest islands are still slightly crisp, though they recede well when the picture is blurred. A warm veil on the farthest one softened it a little, and more veils would turn them grey.
- The wipe ghosts have blended into the water and the dissolving reflection.
- The lily pads are painted in a fairly uniform way.

The main new lesson, recorded in the journal: strokes blended right away in their own direction, inside a soft area where the values already match, become reflections. That holds for light paint as well as dark. The earlier lessons still apply.

final:
I've finished **Evening Gold, Willow Pool**, and my heart is happy with it.

When I came back to it, the picture still held together in normal colour and squinted down. The only thing I felt was missing was evening warmth on the lily pads. They were all a cool yellow-green and didn't connect to the gold sky reflection above them.

**What I did this sitting:**
- **Trial on the near-left island:** short, straight flat-brush touches, not blended, over the dry pads. The peach-ochre touches worked. The salmon-pink ones read as extra flowers, so I wiped them with a small rag. A faint pink trace is left, and I'm keeping it.
- **Warm touches on four islands:** I added a few muted olive-peach touches to the upper parts of the near-left, near-right, mid-right and centre islands. Seen whole, they add a slight evening warmth without making new spots.

**Earlier unresolved points, judged again:**
- **Far islands slightly crisp:** I'm leaving them. They still recede when the picture is blurred.
- **Wipe ghosts from earlier corrections:** I'm leaving them. They've blended into the water.
- **Pads painted too evenly:** the warm touches improve this a little, and I'm leaving the rest as it is.
- **Left-middle island stays cooler:** this is on purpose, because it sits in the willows' shadow.

**Lessons I've carried into the journal:**
- Accents on the pads integrate when they're straight, unblended and close in value. Pinkish ones read as flowers, so pad accents should stay ochre or olive.
- A spirit-soaked rag still lifts fresh paint cleanly off a dry layer, so it works as an undo.
- Opaque, very white dabs that are then blended still look pasted on.
- Thin veils integrate but change little.
- Vertical strokes blended straight away in the same direction still read as reflections.

final:
I've finished **Evening Gold, Willow Pool**, and my heart is happy with it.

I looked at it fresh, at full size, blurred and in close crops. The picture still holds together. Dark violet-blue willow reflections hang on either side of a gold sky reflection. Lilac water runs down into a deep blue foreground. Seven lily-pad islands float on it, with pink and white flowers.

**What I did this sitting:** under the far island I found two small dark-blue marks that looked like stray "legs" hanging off it. With the paint dry, I covered them with a few short horizontal touches of a pale lilac mixed from colours I already had. Seen whole, the spot is gone. Up close a faint trace is left, which reads as a slight reflection under the island, so I'm keeping it.

**Earlier unresolved points, judged again:**
- **Far islands slightly crisp:** I'm leaving them. They still recede when the picture is blurred.
- **Wipe ghosts:** I'm leaving them. They've blended into the water.
- **Pads painted fairly evenly:** I'm leaving them. Last sitting's warm touches already vary them enough.
- **Left-middle island stays cooler:** this is on purpose, because it sits in the willows' shadow.

**Lessons I've carried into the journal:**
- A rag soaked in spirits lifts fresh paint cleanly off a dry layer, so it works as an undo.
- Opaque, very white dabs that are then blended look pasted on.
- Thin veils blend in well but change little.
- Vertical strokes blended straight away in the same direction read as reflections.
- Accents on the pads should be straight, unblended, close in value, and ochre or olive rather than pink.
- A small stray mark can be covered with short touches of a colour mixed to match its surroundings, kept off the neighbouring shapes.

I'm stopping here because more touches would start to fuss a picture whose strength is its softness.

I've finished **Evening Gold, Willow Pool**, and my heart is happy with it.

Coming back with fresh eyes, I first checked every point I'd left unresolved, in close crops:
- **Far islands:** I'm leaving them. They still recede.
- **The small repair under the far island:** I'm leaving it. The faint trace still reads as a reflection.
- **Wipe ghosts:** I'm leaving them. They've dissolved into the water.
- **Fairly even pads:** I'm leaving them as they are.
- **Cooler left-middle island:** this is on purpose, because it sits in the willows' shadow.

**One new thing:** at full size, the bottom of the right willow reflection ended in a hard, jagged edge above a pale strip. It read a little like a rocky bank, the same problem the left side used to have. I fixed it with the method that had already worked twice on the edges of the gold reflection. I laid a few vertical violet-green strokes, starting inside the dark and running down past the edge, and blended them straight down with a soft brush while they were still wet. The willow now seems to hang down into the water toward the small island on the right. Blurred, the right side dissolves the way the left one does. One streak is slightly magenta up close, and I'm keeping it. I stopped after two small patches so the streaks wouldn't line up into a row of pillars.

The picture is still dark violet-blue willow reflections hanging on either side of a gold sky reflection. Lilac water runs down into a deep blue foreground, and seven lily-pad islands float on it with pink and white flowers. The journal has the updated handoff and the lessons that still apply.

final:
**Evening Gold, Willow Pool** is finished, and my heart is happy with it. I didn't add any paint this sitting.

I looked at the whole canvas fresh, at full size, squinted (blurred) and in gallery light, and in close crops. Then I checked each point I'd left open last time:

- **Right willow streaks:** I'm leaving them. They hang into the water toward the small right island without lining up into a row of pillars. The one slightly magenta streak doesn't show from a normal distance.
- **Far island and the small repair under it:** I'm leaving them. The pale marks below the island still read as the gold reflected in the water.
- **Rag-wipe ghosts:** I'm leaving them. The rectangular one in the lower water has disappeared into the ripples, and the streaks under the left willow read as the reflection fading out.
- **Fairly even pads and the cooler left-middle island:** I'm leaving them. The cooler island is on purpose, because it sits in the willows' shadow.

Blurred, the picture still holds together. Dark violet-blue willow reflections hang on either side of a gold column of reflected sky. The water turns from lilac to deep blue toward the front, and seven lily-pad islands with pink and white flowers float on it, getting smaller as they recede. I didn't find anything I wanted to take further, and more touches would start to fuss a picture whose strength is its softness.

The journal has the final handoff and the practical lessons that still apply.
